narrative:
The model estimates you have a 17% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three factors that pulled the outcome toward failure. First, your record shows no past class failures, which is exactly average for students who passed; however, the model sees this as unexpectedly neutral and it actually reduced the chance of success compared with similar students. Second, although you clearly want to pursue higher education, this ambition is shared by every student who passed, so it provides no extra push toward success in your case and slightly lowered the predicted outcome. Third, your mother works as a teacher. While many successful students also have parents in education-related roles, in your specific combination of circumstances this background contributed a modest pull toward the failing side.

Taken together, these elements outweighed several positive signals such as your good family relationships, internet access at home, and desire to continue studying. Because the risk is above the passing threshold, remedial courses are mandatory to strengthen the areas the model flagged.

To improve, focus on building consistent daily study habits beyond your current less-than-two-hours per week, reduce your eight absences (more than double the average of students who passed), and turn your ambition for higher education into concrete actions such as regular homework and seeking extra academic support. Small, steady changes now can shift your trajectory before the final exams.
